newsitem.title: UK: Euro Eurobonds to blossom as first issues take root.
newsitem.headline: Euro Eurobonds to blossom as first issues take root.

text.p: The first Euro Eurobonds have already appeared and bankers on Tuesday said that after a smooth inception investors can expect more deals in coming months.

Three such bonds -- which have been sold in a European currency and will be redenominated in euros after EMU -- have appeared in quick succession, suggesting to bankers that more deals were waiting in the wings.
"If we've done (a euro Eurobond) and other banks have as well, you can be sure everybody else is working on it," said the head of capital markets at a leading Eurobond house.
Preparations for the euro deals have been lengthy, up to six months, because of legal complexities.

However, the end product is straightforward. A key clause from a pioneering bond by Austria launched on January 13 in French francs said: "The issuer will have the option to redenominate the Notes in euros".
A syndicate manager at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam, one of the five banks to be involved so far in lead managing a euro Eurobond, said the market has been slow to take off so far.

"Banks have only just begun picking up on (EMU) even though we're only 22 months away," he said. "(Investor) perception was that the single currency was still a long way away. Momentum was very slow to build up."

But the three euro deals launched so far have attuned investor perception more closely to the next stage of European economic and monetary union and the likely introduction of a single currency for several EU nations, dealers said.
The rationale behind the deals is that Eurobonds in currencies like the mark and French franc will become illiquid when various government bond markets are redenominated post-EMU.

J.P. Morgan, which lead-managed Austria in francs, said that while parts of the Eurobond market would become fragmented after EMU, euro bonds would be super liquid because of their size and because of the pan-European aspect.
All three bonds launched so far include language allowing them to be fungible with other issues the borrower might launch in the future, creating jumbo euro Eurobonds.

In the interim, the three deals, Austria's and two from the European Investment Bank, will be traded as ordinary Eurobonds in their underlying currency until the euro is adopted when they will be redenominated.
Redenominating outstanding Eurobonds is not a viable option, dealers said, given the logistical difficulties and the expense.
Traders at several banks not yet directly involved in euro deals were quick to belittle the redenomination concept, saying it was a launch gimmick.
Gimmick or not, the deals have sold well to institutional investors, the targeted audience, and the borrowers will have been pleased with the results.
Austria, a small country which will have to fight to attract capital in the pan-European market after EMU, will now be a better understood credit to French investors, J.P. Morgan said.
The EIB, which unreservedly sees EMU going ahead on January 1, 1999, has a slightly different agenda.
It sees its role as both a borrower and lender expanding after EMU and it wants investors to know there can be no questioning the liquidity of its paper.
ABN AMRO, lead manager of a 1.0 billion guilder-into-euro offering for the EIB, said it wanted to make a "significant statement" with the fungible deal.
EIB chairman Brian Unwin told Reuters last December that in some situations after EMU, "I can see that the EIB might be called on to a greater extent to help finance investment".
French state-owned Caisse des Depots et Consignations, Paribas and SBC Warburg, joint lead managers on the EIB's second deal, said it was oversubscribed several times.
Demand had been overwhelming "for what is a very large, liquid issue," a syndicate manager at SBC Warburg said.
